functionalObligations.text: a person may not trade until an account is opened at the regulated exchange and passes identity and geographic eligibility screening
functionalObligations.note: approximate: `Aw` names a permission/identity gate, but this is an account-opening process at a regulated broker-exchange, enforced off-chain and continuously by a compliance function, not a transfer-time eligibility check on a claim. Corpus marker retained.

functionalObligations.text: orders rest in a continuous two-sided limit order book operated by the exchange, quoted in sub-penny dollar prices and published as bids only
functionalObligations.note: residue. `Ob` is an ON-CHAIN order book and nothing here is on-chain: the book, the matching engine and the record of positions are proprietary rows in Kalshi's system (KalshiEX Rule 6.2). The corpus reached the same conclusion by the wrong route — it called this 'a conventional off-exchange matching engine'; it is in fact an on-exchange CLOB run by the DCM with a documented public API (stage-1 delta 2). The conclusion survives the correction.

functionalObligations.text: the long and short of one contract are complementary claims on one escrowed dollar, and that complementarity exists only as a price identity — a YES bid at X is a NO ask at $1.00 minus X — with no object that can be split into or merged out of the pair
functionalObligations.note: residue, and the negative half of the category's first structural claim. Nothing in the 58 splits collateral into complementary contingent claims along a state partition; `Py` splits a claim along time and takes no partition argument. Kalshi shows that the primitive can be dispensed with entirely — the complement is an identity in the price domain, not an object — and the vocabulary cannot name that arrangement either, because it has no symbol for a position that exists only as a venue's bookkeeping row.

functionalObligations.text: no trade is accepted unless the account already holds the collateral for it: an event contract is collateralised against its Maximum Downside Exposure before clearing, and a margined contract against initial margin computed over a regulatory liquidation horizon with anti-procyclicality measures
functionalObligations.note: approximate: `Ct` names the margin/LTV/health computation, and this is exchange-rule margin computed off-chain by the DCO under CFTC Reg. 39.13(g), gross per member with no netting across FCM customers. The pre-trade refusal branch — the clearing house declines the transaction rather than opening a position that can later fail a test — has no separate symbol.

functionalObligations.text: on acceptance of a matched trade the clearing house is substituted as seller to the buying participant and buyer to the selling participant, the original bilateral contract is extinguished, and the parties are released from their obligations to each other
functionalObligations.note: residue, and the category's second structural claim stated precisely (Klear DCO Rule 6.1(E)(1); KalshiEX Rule 6.1(c)). Nothing in the 58 is a counterparty-substitution operator. `Rd` names a $1 payment right but carries no obligor identity, and the identity of the obligor is the entire content of novation. Consent is constructive on both sides — participants consent by entering orders, the clearing house by accepting the trade — which no delegation symbol (`Au`) reaches either.

functionalObligations.text: open margined positions are marked and settled in cash at least once each business day, with unscheduled intra-day calls available
functionalObligations.note: residue. Klear Rules 6.2(A), 7.2, 7.4. `Ct` names the test that triggers the call, not the periodic cash transfer that realises the mark. `Pf` is the nearest transfer in the vocabulary and is a funding payment tethering a perpetual to an index, not a daily realisation of profit and loss on a dated contract. Nothing names periodic mark-to-market settlement.

functionalObligations.text: at expiration a binary contract pays the $1.00 Settlement Value to the side whose Payout Criterion is met, by the clearing house debiting its settlement account and crediting member accounts
functionalObligations.note: approximate, and the corpus marker is now citable rather than asserted (stage-1 delta 3: Klear Rule 6.2(C), KalshiEX Rule 6.3(d)(b)). `Rd` names an unconditional right to be paid, but the payment is a clearing-house bookkeeping entry against a segregated settlement account, not a redemption against a reserve, and the right is against an institution `Rd` cannot name (see F5).

functionalObligations.text: a scalar contract apportions the $1.00 between long and short as a function of where the Expiration Value falls, rather than paying it wholly to one side
functionalObligations.note: residue. The apportionment rule — a continuous division of one unit of collateral between two counterparties as a function of an observed value — is not `Op`: there is no premium, no writer, no strike and no uncollateralised leg, and the two sides are symmetric. `Rd` (F7) names each side's right to collect but not the rule that decides how much.

functionalObligations.text: members fund a mutualised guaranty fund sized so the clearing house survives the default of the member creating the largest exposure in extreme but plausible conditions, cash only, at least $1,000,000 for a new member
functionalObligations.note: approximate but sound; stage 1 confirms the mapping (Rule 12.4). `Bs` is slashable first-loss capital and the guaranty fund is applied to another member's default rather than slashed for the depositor's own fault, and the deposit requirement is recomputable by a risk committee at any time — a discretionary sizing `Bs` does not carry.

functionalObligations.text: the operator commits two capped tranches of its own capital to the default waterfall, one ahead of the mutualised fund and one behind it, each capped at the greater of $20 million or 10% of the guaranty fund
functionalObligations.note: residue; stage-1 finding beyond the corpus record (Rule 12.5(C)(2)-(5)). Operator first-loss is structurally unlike `Bs`: it is not staked by a third party, not slashable by rule, and not a pool — it is a capped contractual obligation of one named firm, and it appears TWICE in the ordering, sandwiching the mutualised layer. Nothing in the 58 names a first-loss commitment by the venue itself, and nothing names a loss-absorption ORDER over heterogeneous sources.

functionalObligations.text: when the fund is exhausted the clearing house may call assessments on every surviving member, pro rata to their deposit requirement over the preceding three months, capped at 200% for one default and 550% for multiple defaults in six months, and refundable pro rata out of later recoveries
functionalObligations.note: residue; stage-1 finding beyond the corpus record. Callable capital is neither pre-posted collateral (`Bs`) nor loss socialisation (`Sl`): it is a contingent claim the clearing house holds AGAINST its members, unfunded until called, capped, and reversible on recovery. No element expresses an obligation to pay that does not yet exist.

functionalObligations.text: if resources remain short after assessments, unpaid variation-margin gains owed to members are haircut
functionalObligations.note: Rule 12.5(D). Good fit: a residual loss is assigned to a defined claim class (members owed gains this cycle). Note the rulebook's own carve-out — haircutting and tear-ups 'are not Assessments and are therefore not subject to the Assessment limits' — so the uncapped tail sits in `Sl` and `Ad`, not in the capped instruments.

functionalObligations.text: as the last resort the clearing house tears up open contracts to close the book
functionalObligations.note: Rule 12.5(E). `Ad` (rank-ordered forced close) is the intended reconstruction and fits: tear-ups extinguish the winning side's contracts to match the shortfall.

functionalObligations.text: the mutualised default fund is partitioned by Contract Segment between the fully-collateralised and margined product classes, and the collateral of non-defaulting customers in each account class may not be applied to a defaulting member's obligations
functionalObligations.note: residue (Rules 12.4, 12.5(C)(1)(a)). Two distinct fences, neither named. `Im` fences an isolated LENDING market; there is no symbol for segmenting a mutualised default fund by product class, and none for a legal ring-fence around one claimant class's collateral inside a single custodian.

functionalObligations.text: the outcome of a contract is determined by an internal committee of the exchange with full discretion, within 24 hours, and its determination is final and not subject to review
functionalObligations.note: residue (KalshiEX Rules 6.3(c), 7.1). This is a tribunal and the vocabulary has no symbol for one. `Oa` requires an assertion, a bond and a dispute window and there is none of the three; `Ex` requires a data feed and a medianizer and there is neither; `Sv` is written for servicing a loan, not for adjudicating a fact with finality. Disagreement about an outcome here is not adjudicated, it is decided.

functionalObligations.text: where the Expiration Value is indeterminable the contract may be settled at its own last traded price
functionalObligations.note: residue (Rule 6.3(c)(a)). A self-referential settlement: the market's own final price becomes the payout, so the order book is the oracle. `Tp` (on-chain time-weighted price) is the nearest shape and is not it — no time weighting, no on-chain series, and the price being consulted is the price of the very claim being settled.

functionalObligations.text: after the first day of trading the venue may designate a new Source Agency and Underlying for a listed contract and change its specifications
functionalObligations.note: residue (KalshiEX Rule 7.2(a)). A mutable oracle DESIGNATION, distinct from `Up` (a mutable implementation) and from `Ex` (a feed). The instrument's settlement source is a venue parameter, so what the contract means can change while it is open.

functionalObligations.text: a new market exists because the venue self-certified its terms with the regulator under CEA 5c(c) and the regulator did not object within the window
functionalObligations.note: residue, confirming the corpus. `Aw` gates USERS; this is an authority gate on INSTRUMENTS, and it is a negative permission — listing succeeds by the absence of an objection. The listed product itself is a natural-language Payout Criterion plus a named Source Agency, i.e. a rulebook, for which there is also no symbol.

functionalObligations.text: the venue charges a taker fee of ceil(M x 0.07 x C x P x (1-P)) and a maker fee of ceil(M x 0.0175 x C x P x (1-P)) per trade, debited from member accounts into a clearing-house proprietary account, with no settlement fee
functionalObligations.note: approximate, and a departure from the corpus element set, which recorded no fee element for Kalshi. `Fd` (candidate register) names the taking and distribution of a fee; here the whole surplus accrues to one residual claimant, the operator. The pricing rule itself — a fee proportional to P(1-P), i.e. to the variance of the contract — has no analogue in any fee element.

functionalObligations.text: the venue lists perpetual futures on crypto prices with leverage up to 5.8x and a funding rate rebalanced three times a day on an eight-hour cycle against a reference price the exchange selects
functionalObligations.note: departure from the corpus, which recorded Kalshi as a purely binary, purely fully-collateralised venue (stage-1 delta 1). `Pf` names the funding transfer and the shape is right, but the framing is not: the rate is computed by the venue, the leverage caps are set by the venue, and the reference price is selected by the venue with no feed, no aggregation and no medianizer. That leaves L1a and L4 unsatisfiable for this construction — both demand a truth element (Ex|Tp|Oa|At) beside `Pf`, and Kalshi has none, because its truth source is a committee (F15). The unsatisfied law is the finding, not a defect in the spec. Whether the perpetuals clear in the margined tier rather than the fully-collateralised one is an inference from the existence of leverage, not a documented mapping; stage 1 marks it UNKNOWN.

functionalObligations.text: the exchange and the clearing house may invoke Emergency Rules to suspend or modify trading and clearing
functionalObligations.note: approximate (Klear Rule 2.12; KalshiEX Rule 2.8). `Gp` names an emergency guardian or pause and the function matches, but the guardian is a corporate board acting off-chain under a rulebook with no enumerated trigger set and no on-chain effect, and its powers are broader than halting — it may modify terms.

functionalObligations.text: customer funds are held in United States dollars only, segregated by account class under CFTC Reg. 1.20 or Part 22 with the clearing house holding a continuing first-priority security interest and UCC control over them, investable only in US Treasuries, agency securities, reverse repo on those and government money-market funds up to two-year maturity — and the clearing house retains all profit from that investment not paid to members
functionalObligations.note: residue (Rules 7.6, 7.7, 7.9); stage 1 records segregation and the float as one finding — assets held for a claimant whose income belongs to the custodian. Nothing in the 58 names custody at all, `Fz` (freeze / forced transfer) names a seizure event rather than a standing lien, and `Sh` and `Ix` both assume the yield on pooled assets accrues to the claim, which here it explicitly does not. This is the venue's float business.

paper.title: Kalshi
paper.label: cat:prd:kalshi
paper.blurb: A user opens an account at a regulated exchange and buys a contract on a stated future fact, at a price that reads directly as a probability. At expiration the contract pays a fixed settlement value to the side whose payout criterion is met; a scalar contract apportions that value between long and short rather than paying it whole, and either way the payment is a clearing-house bookkeeping entry against a segregated settlement account. The outcome is determined by the exchange itself. An internal committee interprets the contract's terms with full discretion and its determination is final and not subject to review, so a disagreement about an outcome is not adjudicated but \emph{decided}; where the fact is indeterminable the contract may settle at its own last traded price, and once trading has begun the venue may designate a different settlement source for a contract that is already open.
paper.witnessReason: The corpus records $Aw$, $Ct$ and $Rd$. The witness adds $Bs$, $Sl$ and $Ad$ because the clearing rulebook specifies a default waterfall in more detail than any other document in the corpus --- a mutualised guaranty fund, variation-margin gains haircutting, and tear-ups --- and adds $Pf$, $Fd$ and $Gp$ because the venue now lists perpetual futures with a funding rate, publishes a fee schedule computed from the contract's own price, and holds emergency powers under both the exchange and the clearing rulebook. Among the alternatives the loss-absorption term leaves open, the rulebook names its own layers in its own order, so the witness follows the rulebook rather than the nearest DeFi analogue. The construction is rejected, and the rejection is correct: every element that could close the truth term requires a feed, a price series or an independent attester, and the truth source here is a committee.
paper.residueNote: What the construction cannot say is the institution. Novation extinguishes a bilateral obligation and replaces it with obligations against a clearing house, and nothing in the vocabulary is a counterparty-substitution operator: $Rd$ names a right to be paid and carries no obligor, and the obligor is the entire content of novation. Beyond it, the operator's own capped first-loss contributions and the callable assessments the clearing house may levy on surviving members --- unfunded until called, capped, and refundable out of later recoveries --- have no symbol either, so the vocabulary reconstructs the mutualised middle of this waterfall and neither end of it. The rest of the residue is the product: a payout criterion written in prose, a settlement source the venue may replace mid-contract, a listing that exists because a regulator did not object, and customer money whose investment income belongs to its custodian. This is the most precisely specified default waterfall in the corpus, and that precision is what makes its inexpressibility a result rather than an omission.
